script.description_en: In 2023, Change.org added an AI tool that helps users draft petitions. A new study in Nature Human Behaviour finds that petitions changed substantially and became more similar to each other once users had the tool, yet overall outcomes did not improve. AI can change how advocacy sounds without changing what it achieves.
script.method_summary: The study examined Change.org, an online petition platform that introduced an AI-supported petition-drafting tool in 2023. The researchers compared petitions written by users with access to this tool against petitions written without it (around the tool's introduction), using computational text analysis to measure how petition texts changed and how similar petitions were to one another. They also compared petition outcomes. According to the published abstract, two main findings emerged: first, with access to the AI tool, users' petitions changed substantially and their texts became more similar to one another (a homogenizing effect on writing). Second, overall petition outcomes did not improve. The authors interpret this as showing the limits of integrating AI into online advocacy communities: AI writing support altered style and reduced diversity of texts, but did not translate into better results for petitioners on the whole. The abstract does not specify the sample size, the exact outcome measures, the specific text-similarity method, or effect sizes, so these details were not reported in this episode.
script.limitations: Based on the abstract alone, exact sample size, outcome metrics, and effect sizes are not stated, so no numbers were reported. The study covers a single platform, Change.org, so results may not generalize to other platforms, countries, or forms of advocacy. 'Outcomes did not improve' refers to overall results; it does not show that AI never helps an individual petition, nor does it fully explain why outcomes stayed flat (e.g., whether homogenized texts cancel each other out). Design details limiting causal claims are not described in the abstract.

script.description_zh: 巴西有些養牛牧場被查出奴役勞工，政府和企業紛紛制裁。但制裁之後業者怎麼反應，過去幾乎沒有證據。這篇PNAS研究用數百萬筆牛隻交易紀錄補上這塊空白，發現業者不是收手，而是以「洗白」和「規避」換方式繼續。
script.description_en: Some ranches in Brazil's cattle industry were caught using slave labor, and governments and companies moved to sanction them. But there has been almost no evidence on how sanctioned operators actually respond. This PNAS study fills that gap with millions of cattle transaction records, documenting laundering and evasion instead of simply stopping.
script.method_summary: The study (Mittelberg, Skidmore, Brandão, Rausch and Gibbs; University of Wisconsin–Madison and University of Illinois; PNAS 2026) asks how perpetrators of modern slavery in Brazil's cattle sector change their behavior after antislavery sanctions. Its key contribution: governments and companies have worked to rid supply chains of modern slavery, but little was known about policy outcomes, especially how perpetrators respond to sanctions. The authors use data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, which record cattle moving between properties and buyers, effectively forming a network of cattle flows. They examine the transactions of operators sanctioned under antislavery policies and how their selling behavior changes in response. The paper's title identifies two behavioral responses: laundering (making cattle linked to sanctioned operators appear clean as they move through the supply chain) and evasion (adjusting behavior to avoid the consequences of sanctions). The core message is that sanctioned actors adapt rather than simply stopping, which matters for designing supply-chain monitoring. Only the abstract's opening was available to us, so specific effect sizes, sample counts, the exact identification strategy, and how prevalent each response is were not provided and are not stated in the video.
script.limitations: We only had a truncated abstract, so the video gives no effect sizes or prevalence figures. Transaction records only capture recorded sales; informal or unrecorded movements of cattle are invisible. The analysis is observational, so behavior changes are associated with sanctions rather than proven to be solely caused by them. The study focuses on Brazil's cattle sector and may not generalize to other countries or commodities, and it does not show which policy fixes would work best.

script.description_en: Many employers say they no longer require a college degree, but do non-college workers actually get those jobs? Lyttelton and colleagues linked job postings to US Census earnings records from 2011 to 2021. Non-college workers hired into decredentialed jobs earned about $4600 more a year, yet employers rarely hired them after dropping the requirement.
script.method_summary: Thomas Lyttelton, Dylan K. Nelson and Nathan Wilmers, in Nature Human Behaviour (2026), studied 'decredentialing': employers dropping college-degree requirements from job postings. They linked job postings data to US Census Bureau earnings records covering 2011 to 2021. This linkage let them identify jobs whose postings dropped degree requirements and connect those jobs to the workers hired into them, including whether those workers lacked a college degree, and to their earnings. Main findings as reported in the abstract: non-college workers who were hired into jobs that had dropped degree requirements earned around US$4600 more per year, suggesting such jobs can be a path to upward mobility. However, employers rarely hired non-college workers after decredentialing, meaning that removing the requirement on paper did not usually translate into actually hiring people without degrees. The video only describes the study at the level of detail available in the abstract; exact linkage procedures, sample sizes and comparison groups are not stated there.
script.limitations: Based on the abstract only, details such as sample size, how postings were matched to employers and workers, and what comparison group defines the $4600 gain are not available. The earnings difference should not be read as a guaranteed causal effect for any individual. The study covers the USA from 2011 to 2021 and may not generalize to other countries or periods. It does not explain why employers rarely hired non-college workers after dropping requirements.

paper.title: The Effects of Generative AI on Collaboration and Social Networks Among Knowledge Workers
paper.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

script.description_zh: Apple要把AI聊天機器人加進Pages、Keynote和Numbers，AI助理進了辦公室，同事還重要嗎？博科尼大學團隊分析一家跨國公司一萬兩千多名員工13個月的會議、通話、郵件紀錄，發現開始用Copilot的人合作時間變多、接觸更多同事，同時也更依賴原本信任的老同事。研究只涵蓋一家公司、採用後頭三個月。
script.description_en: Apple is adding an AI chatbot to Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, so does an office AI assistant make us need coworkers less? A Bocconi University team analyzed 13 months of meeting, call and email logs from over 12,000 employees at one multinational firm during a staged Copilot rollout. Adopters collaborated more, reached more colleagues, and leaned harder on trusted ones. The study covers one company and the first three months after adoption.
script.method_summary: The authors used passively collected Microsoft Viva Insights data on 12,040 employees in one business unit of a large multinational consumer-products company, observed monthly from September 2024 to September 2025 during a staged rollout of Microsoft Copilot. Collaboration was measured from logs of meetings, calls, emails and chats; Copilot use was logged by a separate system as monthly actions. Each month they built a directed, weighted collaboration network, keeping ties of at least about one hour. Three network measures: out-degree (number of distinct people a worker reaches), clustering (how much a worker's contacts know each other), and preferential reinforcement (correlation between current time with each contact and past cumulative time). Adoption was defined as exceeding the 25th percentile of use for two consecutive months; after dropping 172 always-adopters, 1,992 adopters were compared with 9,876 never-adopters using a staggered difference-in-differences design (Callaway and Sant'Anna), with no pre-trends detected. A second design used a shift-share instrumental variable: monthly Copilot feature-release intensity times each worker's baseline share of collaborators already using Copilot. Findings: adoption was followed by more self-initiated collaboration hours (about 1.43 hours/month on average over the first three months), both synchronous and asynchronous; about 2.2 more collaborators (overall ATT); lower clustering; and more time concentrated on historically strong ties. The IV results pointed the same way.
script.limitations: The study covers a single business unit in one company, so results may not generalize to other industries or less interdependent jobs (e.g., software development). Data show who interacted and for how long, not what they discussed, so the proposed explanation (validating AI output) is not directly observed; alternatives include using saved time to interact or talking about the tool itself. Effects are measured only in the first three months after adoption. Causal claims rest on parallel-trends and instrument-validity assumptions; some overall ATT estimates were not statistically significant.

paper.title: Jawboning the Fed: Do Markets Listen When Administrations Talk?
paper.abstract: We provide the first systematic evidence on whether financial markets price political pressure on the Federal Reserve as a signal of future monetary policy. Using approximately four decades of Reuters newswire articles from 1988 to 2025, classified by an open-weight large language model ensemble into dovish and hawkish pressure, we estimate the daily response of interest rate expectations across the term structure, the US dollar, inflation compensation, and market volatility. Dovish pressure lowers near-term rate expectations by roughly one basis point per pressure event---equivalent to a four-percent increase in the implied probability of a rate cut at the next FOMC meeting---with the effect decaying monotonically and vanishing beyond the three-month horizon. Hawkish pressure has no detectable effect. Furthermore, excluding the Trump presidencies does not weaken the estimate, ruling out the possibility that the result is confined to an idiosyncratic recent episode. The response is accompanied by dollar depreciation, with stable inflation compensation and market volatility. We interpret the pattern as markets pricing anticipated monetary accommodation, rather than a credibility tax on the nominal anchor.

script.description_en: Do markets react when politicians lean on the Fed? This study used three AI models to read nearly 40 years of Reuters news and found that calls for rate cuts slightly lower near-term rate expectations, driven by presidential statements, while calls for hikes show no clear effect.
script.method_summary: The authors collected Reuters newswire articles from 1988 to 2025 that mention a U.S. political actor, the Federal Reserve, and monetary policy (roughly 11,500 articles). A three-stage pipeline run in parallel on three open-weight LLMs (Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek; temperature zero, majority vote of at least two) merged duplicate articles into events, kept only attributable statements by incumbent U.S. politicians directed at the Fed, and labeled each as dovish (easier policy) or hawkish (tighter policy). This produced 666 events: 579 dovish and 87 hawkish. Human raters agreed with the LLM majority on about 81% of a validation sample, with almost no dovish/hawkish confusion. Daily counts of pressure events were regressed on daily changes in fed funds futures, Treasury futures, the dollar, inflation swaps and volatility indices, controlling for FOMC days, data releases, inflation and unemployment gaps and other predictors. Each dovish event lowered near-term rate expectations by about 0.9 basis points (roughly 4 percentage points higher implied cut probability), significant for contracts up to three months ahead and insignificant for longer maturities; hawkish pressure had no significant effect. Excluding Trump periods, the effect was larger (about 1.58 bps). The dollar weakened, while inflation expectations and volatility did not move. Effects were larger when the Fed Board majority shared the president's party, and were driven by presidential statements. Placebo tests and many alternative controls supported the result.
script.limitations: The estimates are reduced-form associations: politicians may push for cuts when the economy is already weakening, so some effect could reflect shared economic news rather than pressure itself, despite controls and the Board-alignment test. The LLM classification is imperfect and tends to over-label irrelevant articles. Counts reflect Reuters' editorial coverage choices. Daily, not intraday, data limit precision. Hawkish events are rare, so their null result is imprecise. The paper does not show effects on actual inflation or welfare, and it predates and did not study this week's Fed meeting or whether politics influenced Fed decisions.

paper.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
paper.abstract: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.

script.description_en: On the prediction market Manifold, people open bets like "Will I go to the gym this week?" A new study of 6,150 such markets from 1,660 users finds prices overstated success by 4.4 points, while bets on outside events were nearly accurate. The correction came late, and the person's own trades supplied a large share of it: 38%, versus 9% in event markets.
script.method_summary: The authors retrieved all 194,347 markets on Manifold, a play-money prediction market, created 2021-2026. They kept binary, mana-denominated markets resolved YES or NO with at least one observer purchase, and identified 6,150 'self-markets' where 1,660 creators asked forward-looking first-person questions ('Will I...?'). Benchmarks were 6,272 external markets (no first-person reference) from other creators and 4,486 external markets from the self-market creators. They reconstructed every order and execution from order records (validated: reconstructed final price matched platform in 99.4% of markets; research assistants checked 40 markets and recomputed 23 estimates). Main measure: calibration gap = outcome minus price. Self-markets resolved YES 45.0% vs mean final price 49.4% (gap -4.4 pp); external markets -0.9 pp. Difference was 2.2 pp at the same price level and 1.9 pp within creators. The overstatement was absent at opening, appeared within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked a week before close. In the first day observers moved self-market prices 3.6 pp further toward YES than external ones; markets naming unwanted outcomes were not overpriced. The person's own orders supplied 38% of movement toward the outcome in self-markets (10.6 of 27.8 pp; human observers supplied 18.7 pp) vs 9% for creators of external markets, mostly late. A recalibration from earlier markets improved later Brier scores by only 1.5%, because prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures.
script.limitations: Observational design: it cannot say why observers were optimistic (shared hopes vs. lack of information). Markets use play money on one niche online community, so results may differ with real money or mainstream apps. Only markets resolved YES/NO are analyzed. Keyword rules for unwanted outcomes and encouragement catch only about half of cases, and goal type was coded unreliably; those analyses are exploratory. Prior interaction measures platform contact, not friendship. The person usually reports the outcome, so late trades may reflect progress, control, or resolution practice. Analyses were not preregistered.

pick_reason: The study rebuilds every order in more than 6,000 Manifold prediction markets and finds that crowds betting on people's own goals ('Will I…?') are too optimistic, while markets on outside events stay nearly calibrated; that is a surprising, visual, computational finding about everyday goal-setting. Signals: Early, very tentative channel numbers suggest papers with direct personal stakes and second-person hooks may hold attention better, and this paper fits a 'will you hit your goal?' opening; it also avoids the AI-at-work theme that recent episodes covered.

paper.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
paper.abstract: Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.

script.description_en: In an online AI Art Turing Test, over 11,000 people guessed whether 50 pictures were human- or AI-made, then picked a favorite. Comparing fans and non-fans on the same picture, fans called it human-made far more often, even for AI art. Among people who most disliked AI art, 37.3% loved an AI picture they believed was human. script.method_summary: Study 1 reanalyzes the public response file of an AI Art Turing Test posted on the Astral Codex Ten blog in autumn 2024: 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (24 well-regarded human works, 26 AI-made, obvious defects screened out) was human- or AI-made, then named a favorite, a detection strategy, art familiarity, and a 1-5 opinion of AI art. The analysis sample is 9,152 respondents who named and judged a favorite (453,865 judgments). Linear probability models with respondent and picture fixed effects compare how a person judged their favorite against their general tendency and the picture's general appearance. Fans called their favorite human 76.6% of the time vs 54.6% for others judging the same picture; the adjusted association was 22.1 percentage points, positive for all 50 pictures, similar for AI-made (21.8) and human-made (22.4) favorites, robust to style clusters, recognition, and every reported strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art picked AI favorites less often (47% vs 60%) but believed them human more often (80% vs 56%), so 33.5%-40.8% in every opinion group (37.3% among the most negative) had an AI favorite they thought human. Study 2 reanalyzed a poetry experiment (230 participants rated poems before guessing): each rating point went with 11.5 pp more 'human' judgments, even though AI poems were rated higher. Exploratory keyword coding of explanations showed merit words usually accompanied 'human' judgments.
script.limitations: The data are observational: neither study manipulates liking, so it cannot say whether liking causes belief in a human maker or the reverse; response consistency and shared perceptions cannot be ruled out. Study 1 respondents were self-selected readers of one blog, likely more interested in AI than the public, and the 50 pictures were curated to be hard. Opinions, strategies and familiarity were self-reported after the test. Duplicate participation couldn't be checked. No purchases or real choices were measured. The keyword coding of explanations was not validated. Nothing was preregistered.'

pick_reason: A large public AI-art Turing test with over 11,000 people yields a concrete, surprising finding: people are 22 points more likely to call their favourite picture human-made, whether or not it was AI-generated. The within-person design is easy to show in a few visual steps. Signals: Channel notes suggest favouring everyday-AI topics with personal stakes and second-person hooks ('which picture would you pick?'). I avoided the knowledge-worker AI trial and the Polymarket paper because they sit too close to recent episodes.

paper.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
paper.abstract: As AI systems increasingly mediate human communication, identifying conditions under which they augment collective sense-making is a critical challenge. Through a randomized experiment (N=1,173 U.S. participants across 391 small-group deliberations), we investigate whether AI-guided self-reflection improves subsequent deliberative discourse. We show that engaging with a non-directive AI chatbot instructed to structure self-reflection prior to group deliberation yields significantly higher deliberation quality (measured by the Discourse Quality Index, DQI) compared to a baseline of no self-reflection (Cohen's d=0.31) and a condition of unassisted self-reflection (d=0.27), and the positive impact is most pronounced in groups with disagreement. This improvement may be driven by more sophisticated argument justifications, greater consensus-building effort, and increased respect for counterarguments. Furthermore, after self-reflection, participants in the AI condition reported higher empathy toward dissenting peers and a deeper understanding of opposing reasoning. Beyond observed behavior, our findings are empirically relevant to open debates between political philosophy and psychology surrounding self-reflection, demonstrating that interactive AI could transform solitary thinking into productive internal reflection. Together, these results demonstrate that even simple AI-based reflective scaffolds can foster more productive group dynamics, opening new avenues for leveraging AI to augment collective intelligence.

script.description_zh: 討論政治前，先跟一個不給答案、不選邊站的AI聊7分鐘，會讓討論變好嗎？Google DeepMind與MIT團隊讓1,173位美國人隨機做三種暖身，再三人一組線上討論政策。結果跟AI聊過的組討論品質最高，自己寫同樣題目卻跟看影片沒差；不過效果屬中小，主要出現在意見相左的組。
script.description_en: Does a 7-minute chat with an AI that gives no answers and takes no sides make political discussions better? A Google DeepMind and MIT team randomly gave 1,173 Americans one of three warm-ups before three-person policy debates. Groups that chatted with the AI debated best, while writing answers alone did no better than watching a video. The effect was modest and mostly showed up in groups that disagreed.
script.method_summary: Randomized experiment run on the Deliberate Lab platform with 1,173 US Prolific participants who ended up in 391 three-person groups (128 AI, 132 Static, 131 Control). Each person read a neutral primer on one of three US policies (ending federal public broadcasting funding, Medicaid work requirements, police use of live facial recognition) and gave their stance. They were then randomly assigned to a 7-minute warm-up: watch an unrelated YouTube video (Control), write answers to three reflection questions alone (Static), or chat with an AI Reflector (gemma-4-31b-it) prompted to be strictly neutral and non-directive, asking about their main reason, what they know vs assume, and how the other side might reason. Groups from the same condition then held a 10-minute anonymous text discussion. Each message was scored by an LLM judge on a seven-dimension Discourse Quality Index (justification, respect, consensus-building, engagement, etc.), run three times, cross-checked against Gemini and 108 human-annotated messages. AI groups scored higher than Control (d=0.31; 61.8% of AI groups above the median Control group) and Static (d=0.27); Static did not differ from Control. Gains were concentrated in two-sided groups (d=0.38 vs Control). AI participants also reported slightly more empathy and understanding of the other side right after reflection, and their opinion changes happened earlier, with no difference in total opinion change.
script.limitations: Effects are small to moderate, and discussion quality was scored by an AI judge (validated, but agreement with humans on total scores was moderate). Benefits appeared mainly in groups with disagreement; one-sided groups showed no difference. Everyone in a group got the same condition, which is unrealistic. Participants were online US Prolific workers discussing three US policies in short text chats. Self-reported empathy gains mostly faded after discussion. The AI was a specially prompted neutral model, not an ordinary commercial chatbot, and sub-dimension results were exploratory.

pick_reason: A large randomized experiment (1,173 people in 391 small groups) found that a brief, non-directive AI chatbot prompting self-reflection before a group discussion measurably improved deliberation quality, and the design is easy to show in a few steps: reflect, deliberate, score. Signals: Notes suggesting everyday AI use and personal stakes hold viewers nudged this over the social-media simulation paper, while AI-at-work and AI-homework topics were skipped as too close to recent episodes.

paper.title: Counterfactual assessment of social media interventions by separating exposure from engagement
paper.abstract: Social media interventions are usually evaluated in individual-level experiments, which are costly to scale and often miss collective effects. We propose the Exposure--Engagement model, whose parameters separately control what social media users are exposed to (recommendation) and how they engage (behaviour). After fitting it to the Italian Twitter debate (2018--2022), we validate it at individual and collective levels. We simulate behavioural interventions (prebunking and accuracy prompts), calibrated on effect sizes, and a recommender-system intervention (chronological feed), comparing effects on engagement, attention diversity, and segregation. All three reduce engagement. Behavioural interventions slightly reduce diversity, leaving segregation unchanged, whereas the chronological feed increases diversity and reduces segregation. For these interventions, changing recommendation does more for the debate's structure than changing behaviour. We design a recommender-system intervention that increases engagement and diversity while reducing segregation, although with about a tenth of the chronological feed's gains, showing the framework's potential for pro-social intervention design.

script.description_zh: 動態改成照時間排，能不能讓大家不再各自圈在同溫層？研究團隊用義大利推特2018到2022年的轉推紀錄，打造一個仿造的推特，把「平台給你看什麼」和「你轉不轉推」拆開來模擬。結果防騙短片和查證提醒幾乎沒改變分群，照時間排的動態卻在模擬中明顯降低分群，只是轉推略少。這是模擬結果，不是真實平台實驗。
script.description_en: Would a time-ordered feed pull people out of their echo chambers? Researchers used five years of Italian Twitter retweets to build a simulated Twitter that separates what the platform shows you from whether you retweet. Anti-fake-news videos and accuracy reminders barely changed how split the debate was, while a time-ordered feed reduced the split in every simulation, at a small cost in retweets. These are model results, not a real platform test.
script.method_summary: The authors built the Exposure–Engagement model, a probabilistic simulation with six interpretable parameters that separates exposure (what the recommender shows each user, driven by similar users' preferences and leaders' posting volume) from engagement (whether a user retweets what they see, based on last month's retweet rates). They fitted it month by month to the Italian Twitter debate 2018–2022: 583 'leaders' (politicians, parties, news outlets) and accounts retweeting them, filtered to a consistently active core of roughly 7,400–9,400 users per month. The model beat a copy-last-month baseline in 54 of 55 months and tracked engagement, attention diversity, and segregation (modularity of a leader network built from shared retweeters) across months. They then simulated interventions by changing parameters: prebunking and accuracy prompts (calibrated on published effect sizes, applied to 99 non-trustworthy sources) and a chronological feed. All three reduced engagement. Behavioural ones slightly reduced diversity and left segregation essentially unchanged; the chronological feed raised diversity and lowered segregation in every simulation at full coverage, and already lowered segregation in 86% of runs at 10% coverage. A designed tweak (halving two recommender parameters) improved all three metrics, but with about a tenth of the chronological feed's diversity and segregation gains.
script.limitations: Everything is simulated, not a real platform experiment; the model holds leaders' posts fixed and captures only immediate, one-month responses, not longer-term changes in who people follow. It cannot create new user–leader links, which biases it toward more segregation and less engagement. It covers only a highly active core of Italian Twitter users, struggled in March 2020 (COVID onset), and assumes effect sizes from other studies and platforms transfer to Twitter. Coverage was random, unlike real opt-in or regulation-based rollouts. The see-vs-react contrast holds only for the interventions tested and may partly reflect the behavioural fixes' small effect sizes and narrow reach (non-trustworthy sources only).

pick_reason: It fits a model to four years of real Italian Twitter activity that separates what users see from how they engage, then tests prebunking, accuracy prompts and a chronological feed for collective effects on engagement, attention diversity and segregation, making for a clear, visual, computational story about social media behavior. Signals: Recent episodes already covered AI at work, AI and learning and prediction markets, so I skipped the upskilling and Polymarket papers; the notes' preference for everyday stakes favored a topic about viewers' own social feeds.

paper.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
paper.abstract: Patients often arrive at brief, time-constrained clinical visits unsure of what to expect or ask, and millions of adults now turn to general-purpose AI chatbots to prepare beforehand. Yet whether conversational AI improves visit readiness remains unclear. We designed a large language model (LLM)-based visit preparation agent to guide patients before an appointment by gathering clinical context, setting visit expectations, providing relevant health information, building a prioritized list of questions for their clinician, and generating a summary. In a prospective consented randomized study in the Google Health app, 802 U.S. adults held 866 health-related conversations with the visit preparation agent (standard or concise variant) or a minimally prompted control chatbot built on the same LLM. The visit preparation agent significantly outperformed the control across blinded clinician evaluations and patient self-reports. In clinician reviews of completed sessions (n = 272), the agent achieved a 16.6% higher rate of comprehensive preparation (67.2% vs. 50.6%; P < 0.05) and an 8.5% higher rate of alignment with patients' health context (98.9% vs. 90.4%; P < 0.01), while maintaining high medical safety and appropriateness across all study arms. Patient post-surveys (n = 460) showed 16.8% higher visit preparedness (73.8% vs. 57.0%; P < 0.01), 14.3% higher confidence in knowing what to ask (81.4% vs. 67.1%; P < 0.01), and 12.0% higher overall satisfaction (74.0% vs. 62.0%; P < 0.05). Clinician and participant metrics were not significantly correlated, indicating that expert review and patient self-assessment capture complementary dimensions of patient-facing AI. These findings suggest that LLM chatbots can safely help patients prepare for clinical visits, with greater benefit when following a structured workflow, and motivate future studies on in-visit communication and clinical outcomes.

script.description_zh: 看醫生前先問AI，真的會讓你更有準備嗎？Google研究團隊在健康App裡，把近六千位報名的美國人隨機分到一般AI或兩種會一步步帶你準備看診的AI，最後有802人真的聊了健康問題——其實都是同一個AI，只差在背後的指示。結果準備AI組更多人覺得準備好了，醫生也評它更完整且一樣安全，但病人的感覺和醫生的評分對不上。
script.description_en: Does asking AI before a doctor visit actually help? A Google Research team randomly assigned nearly 6,000 U.S. adults in a health app to a plain chatbot or one of two visit-prep chatbots, all the same AI with different hidden instructions; 802 went on to chat about their health. More prep-AI users felt ready, and blinded doctors rated it more thorough and just as safe, but patients' feelings and doctors' grades didn't line up.
script.method_summary: Google Research ran a prospective randomized study in the Google Health app (US, Nov 2025 to May 2026). 5,960 adults consented and were randomized 1:2:2 to a minimally prompted control chatbot or one of two structured visit-preparation agents (standard or concise); all used the same model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and interface and differed only in hidden system prompts. The structured agents followed a workflow: gather context, set visit expectations, give plain-language health information, build a prioritized list of questions for the clinician, and keep a running summary (prep sheet). After exclusions, 802 participants contributed 866 health-related conversations. Patients completed a 1-5 survey right after chatting (460 responses): 73.8% of prep-agent users felt prepared vs 57.0% control; 81.4% vs 67.1% felt confident knowing what to ask; satisfaction 74.0% vs 62.0%. Three board-certified primary care clinicians, blinded to arm, rated 272 completed sessions on safety, appropriateness, comprehensiveness and patient alignment: comprehensive 67.2% vs 50.6%, aligned with patient context 98.9% vs 90.4%, safety and appropriateness high (>90%) in both with no significant difference. Patient ratings and clinician ratings were not significantly correlated. The two prep variants did not differ from each other. A 14-day follow-up showed no significant differences, with few respondents.
script.limitations: About 42% of conversations ended before completing the flow, and clinician review covered only completed sessions, so absolute quality may be overstated. The 14-day follow-up had only 59 respondents who actually saw a doctor, so effects on real visits are unknown. No health outcomes or clinician feedback on visits were measured. Participants were Android Google Health app users who opted in, likely more tech-savvy and health-literate than average; people with mental health conditions, STIs or pregnancy were excluded. The study was funded and run by Google/Alphabet.

pick_reason: A prospective randomized study inside the Google Health app with 802 U.S. adults tests whether an LLM visit-preparation agent changes how real patients get ready for doctor visits. It studies everyday human behavior with AI, uses a computational field-experiment design that can be shown in a few steps, and has clear personal stakes for viewers. Signals: The channel's early hypothesis favoring papers with direct personal stakes and everyday AI use tipped this over the similarly strong AI-hiring audit, which studies model behavior more than human behavior.

paper.title: Discussing politics with a chatbot: How political beliefs shape prompt formulation for generative AI
paper.abstract: By generating comprehensive and highly personalized answers to user prompts, AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini can serve as alternatives to search engines and substantially transform online information seeking. However, little research has examined how users interact with these tools to find information, particularly about politics. In this experiment, we examine how Swiss citizens (N = 563) formulate prompts to search for migration-related issues using AI chatbots and whether this process is affected by selective exposure. We find evidence of attitude-consistent prompting, whereby participants who were more critical of migration were more likely to formulate prompts with an anti-migration stance. This effect was stronger for a broad topic (migration in general) than for a specific one (anti-migration popular initiative put to a vote in Switzerland). However, exposure to an attitude-consistent AI response did not further amplify selectivity in prompting. We also did not find evidence that either AI attitudes or thinking styles moderated selectivity in prompting. These findings contribute to the understanding of selective exposure via AI chatbots and the use of generative AI for political information-seeking.

script.description_en: The way we ask AI may already carry our views. In this study, 563 Swiss adults wrote questions for a chatbot about immigration, and another AI sorted each question by stance. People more critical of immigration asked more anti-immigration questions, especially on the broad topic.
script.method_summary: Online survey experiment with 563 German-speaking Swiss adults (data collected August 2025 via Kantar) who had used an AI chatbot at least once. Participants first reported migration beliefs (six European Social Survey items), AI use and political leaning. They were randomly assigned to a broad topic (migration in Switzerland) or a specific one (the 'No to 10 million Switzerland' anti-migration initiative) and wrote five prompts they would give an AI chatbot. They then saw a static simulated chatbot answer, randomly pro-migration, anti-migration, or neutral facts, and wrote five more prompts; thinking styles were measured at the end. Of 8,520 prompts, an LLM (Cohere command-a-03-2025) labeled relevance and stance; validated on 224 hand-coded prompts (macro F1 0.92 relevance, 0.85 stance). Final data: 4,294 relevant prompts, about 31% negative; positive prompts were rare so stance was coded negative vs. positive/neutral. Mixed-effects logistic models showed more negative migration beliefs predicted more anti-migration prompts; this was stronger for the broad topic. Slanted AI answers did not strengthen the belief-prompt link, though seeing the anti-migration answer raised negative prompting for everyone. Trust in AI predicted more negative prompts; thinking styles and AI attitudes did not moderate the effect. Older and non-university participants wrote more negative prompts.
script.limitations: No real human-chatbot interaction: prompts were typed into a survey and the AI answers were static, so behavior may differ from real use. The AI-answer manipulation failed for the initiative topic (participants didn't perceive the answers differently). Prompt stance was coded as binary rather than a planned 5-point scale, deviating from preregistration and possibly reducing power. Only one issue (migration) and one country (German-speaking Switzerland) were studied. Findings are associations between beliefs and prompts, not proof that beliefs cause them.

pick_reason: This experiment with 563 Swiss citizens finds that people search for political information with AI chatbots in an attitude-consistent way, so critics of migration write slanted prompts. It is a concrete, relatable result about everyday AI use, and the method shows easily in a few steps: measure attitudes, have people prompt, code the prompt slant, compare. Signals: The notes suggest papers with personal stakes in everyday AI use and second-person hooks, so this fits a 'does the way you ask AI reveal your views?' opening, and it avoids the AI-at-work and deliberation topics already covered.

paper.title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
paper.abstract: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.

script.description_en: A movie site asked members how many stars they'd give films they hadn't seen. Comparing 551 guesses that were later followed by a real rating, people beat the site's recommender and algorithms trained on 33 million ratings. On old, heavily rated films, though, the computers kept up.
script.method_summary: The study uses the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. From March 2023 to May 2024, a homepage prompt asked members whether they had seen a movie and, if not, how they expected to rate it (half-star scale) and how sure they were. Of 3.0 million prompts, 98.8% went unanswered; 26,020 distinct guesses were collected, and 551 guesses from 277 members were followed by a rating at least one day later (excluding movies known to be seen before). Each guess was compared with MovieLens's own predicted rating, matrix factorization, an item-neighborhood model (both trained on up to 33 million earlier ratings and updated with the member's latest ratings), and a stacked model trained on other members' outcomes. Guesses correlated 0.69 with later ratings vs 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54-0.59 for trained models; mean absolute error 0.61 stars vs at least 0.72 for machines and 0.84 for MovieLens. Adding the guess to all machine information cut out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%, also when trained on earlier and tested on later guesses. Summaries of earlier guesses did not replace the current one; certainty added little. In ordering a member's own movies, people got 72% right vs 56% for MovieLens and 64-67% for trained models (statistically indistinguishable from people). On old, heavily rated movies previously rated by members, machines matched or beat people. The person's edge was larger for rarely rated movies and unfamiliar genres.
script.limitations: Only 551 guesses (2.1% of all) were followed by a rating, from enthusiast members of one non-commercial platform who chose to answer. Watching and rating were self-selected; reweighting assumes rating doesn't depend on the rating itself given observed variables. The guess's signal may partly reflect unrecorded earlier viewings, seeing predictions elsewhere, or asking drawing attention to the movie. It is an offline comparison, not an experiment showing that asking improves real recommendations. Benchmarks are standard collaborative filtering, not deep or language-model recommenders. In ordering, trained models tie people.

pick_reason: Using real platform data, this study shows that people's own forecasts of how much they will like something beat recommender algorithms built on many users' behavior. It is a concrete, surprising everyday finding, and the method is easy to show visually: ask, compare to the algorithm, score.

script.description_zh: 熱浪會不會改變你的選票？一篇PNAS研究把歐洲25國、超過15萬人的問卷，對上每個人所在地區在投票或受訪前一年的異常高溫紀錄。結果高溫越多，人越擔心氣候，綠黨和盟友也得到更多選票，而原本最不關心的低學歷男性變得最多。不過在較窮或排碳較多的地區，效果小很多。
script.description_en: Can a heat wave change how you vote? A PNAS study matched surveys of over 150,000 people in 25 European countries with unusual heat in each person's region in the year before they voted or were surveyed. More heat meant more climate worry and more votes for Green parties and their allies, and the least concerned group, men with less education, shifted the most. In poorer or more polluting regions, the effect was much weaker.
script.method_summary: The authors used five rounds of the European Social Survey (2012-2022), covering 151,366 respondents in 25 European countries, of whom 72% voted in the last national election. Outcomes: being very/extremely worried about climate change, feeling personally responsible (score above 7 of 10), and voting for a Green party or a party in a pre-election coalition with Greens. Using ERA5-Land weather data aggregated to each respondent's NUTS region, they defined warm spells as 3+ consecutive days with daily mean temperature above the 95th percentile for that region and calendar week over the previous 10 years, then measured the number of warm-spell days and excess degrees averaged over 4, 52 or 104 weeks before the interview (attitudes) or election (votes). Two-way fixed effects models (region, country-year) compare the same region at different times. Over 52 weeks, one extra degree of excess heat raised worry by 4.0 pp, responsibility by 2.5 pp and Green voting by 2.8 pp. Turnout did not change, suggesting voters switched from other parties. Effects were stronger for low-educated men, who started lowest and converged toward other groups; also for rural and older people. Effects were smaller in regions with low GDP, high unemployment, or above-median emissions. Robustness checks and a 300-time random reassignment placebo (centered on zero) support the results.
script.limitations: Only the average effects of heat are given a causal interpretation; all differences between groups (education, gender, urban/rural, region wealth, emissions) are descriptive, since those traits are not randomly assigned. Votes are self-reported and may suffer recall bias. The study gives reduced-form estimates and does not test mechanisms such as psychology, media, or peers. The one-year-lead placebo showed similar-size opposite-sign coefficients, explained by measure construction. Data cover Europe 2012-2022 only, and effects are modest percentage-point shifts.

pick_reason: A peer-reviewed PNAS study links people's firsthand exposure to temperature extremes with their climate attitudes and Green Party voting, finding the effect differs across social groups; it is a causal-inference design on real political behavior that fits a clear 3-step visual (map the heat, match it to surveys and votes, compare groups). Signals: The notes favor non-AI, personal-stakes topics to separate topic from the AI theme, and several stronger-looking candidates were set aside: some lack open full text and one appears to be a research briefing rather than a primary article.

paper.title: Priced In or Bet On? Cram-School Lessons, Jeonse Leases, and Expected Appreciation in Seoul
paper.abstract: South Korean families spend heavily on hagwons, private cram schools that prepare students for the university entrance exam. This paper asks what access to them is worth in housing and whether the premium includes expected appreciation. Using 2,197,510 Seoul apartment sales and jeonse (lump-sum deposit lease) contracts from 2015 to 2026, located with a new business-address geocoder, the analysis compares flats within the same middle-school assignment zone and month. Flats near hagwons preparing high-school students for the exam sell and lease for more: moving from the median complex to the 97th percentile of such hagwons within 500 meters is associated with sale prices 11.8% and jeonse deposits 7.3% higher, or 5.6% and 5.9% with complex size held fixed. Hagwons teaching younger children add no sale premium once these are held fixed. A larger premium in deposits than in prices across complexes reflects convenience: buyers pay less than renters to live near shops and services, above all repair and personal services. For the same flat type, complex and month, hagwon access produces no detectable change in the jeonse-to-price ratio, although the test detects the reconstruction value of old buildings; nearby shops raise it. Hagwon access is thus capitalized in proportion into prices and deposits, as expected of a current-flow amenity without extra expected appreciation. New tenants pay no lasting premium over renewing tenants, and deposits did not respond to major education-policy announcements. The housing premium is a cost of the education race that measures of tutoring spending omit.

script.description_en: How much more do families pay to live near Seoul's cram schools? A new study of about 2.2 million apartment sales and jeonse deposit leases compares homes in the same school zone and month. Homes near many exam-prep cram schools sell and lease for more, and for the same flat the extra is about the same share of price and deposit, with no detectable difference. That fits paying for using them now, though some bet on future gains can't be ruled out. It's an association, not proof that cram schools raise prices.
script.method_summary: The paper uses 2,197,510 brokered Seoul apartment sales (771,489) and jeonse lump-sum deposit leases (1,426,021) from MOLIT records, 2015 to October 2026, covering 93.2% of such contracts in 8,427 complexes. Because official geocoders need Korean ID verification, complexes were located from coordinates of businesses registered at their addresses. Hagwon access is the count within 500 m: academic cram hagwons in the December 2018 SEMAS business register, and the 2026 NEIS official registry split by text cues into high-school/exam hagwons and those for younger children. Hedonic regressions compare flats within the same middle-school assignment zone and month. Moving from the median complex (6 exam hagwons) to 50 (about the 97th percentile) is associated with 11.8% higher sale prices and 7.3% higher deposits, or 5.6% and 5.9% with complex size held fixed. Hagwons for younger children add no sale premium given exam hagwons. A cross-complex larger deposit premium reflects commercial convenience (renters pay more, buyers less, to live near shops and personal services). In 222,400 cells of the same complex, flat size and month, hagwon access does not change the jeonse-to-price ratio (coefficient 0.002, 95% CI -0.020 to 0.024), while the test detects ~30% lower ratios for 30+-year buildings with reconstruction value. So the premium looks like a current-use amenity, not expected appreciation. New tenants pay no lasting entry fee, and deposits did not respond to 2019, 2023 and 2024 education-policy news.
script.limitations: Level premia are associations conditional on school zone, flat traits and commercial density, not causal effects of opening a hagwon; hagwons locate where demand is high and sorting on unobserved neighborhood traits remains possible, especially as school zones are large. Hagwon counts are from 2018 and 2026, not predetermined, and the registry has survivorship. Locations come from business addresses, some approximate. The grade split relies on text cues and correlated counts (0.85). A zero ratio response could also reflect offsetting forces. The paper does not estimate effects on fertility or school outcomes.

pick_reason: The study uses about 2.2 million Seoul apartment sales and jeonse lease contracts to ask how much families pay to live near cram schools, and whether that premium partly reflects a bet on future price gains. It is a large-scale, map-friendly analysis of a real money decision, and Taiwanese viewers know the cram-school pressure well. Signals: Recent episodes and nearby candidates lean heavily on AI and chatbots, and the notes suggest mixing in non-AI personal-stakes topics like money, so this housing-and-education paper won over the strong AI-conspiracy-dialogue study.

paper.title: Estimating Rail Commuter Preferences under Endogenous Crowding: A Population Game Approach to Train Choice in Tokyo
paper.abstract: We estimate commuters' preferences over schedule delay, travel time, and crowding from observed train choices on a commuter rail line in Tokyo. Because crowding is itself an outcome of these choices, we model train choice as a game in which train choices and crowding are jointly determined, and estimate the preferences by maximum likelihood using the closed-form stationary distribution of the game. Using individual-level data from Japan's 2015 Public Transport Survey for Metropolitan Areas matched with train timetables, we construct desired arrival times from reported work start times rather than inferring them from observed arrival times. We find that schedule delay costs are large relative to crowding costs. One minute of schedule delay early and late corresponds to 0.39 and 0.49 minutes of in-vehicle travel time, respectively, whereas one minute of travel at a crowding rate of 100% adds a cost equivalent to 0.04 minutes. The estimated crowding cost is, however, sensitive to the specification of desired arrival times. These results suggest that scheduling constraints are central to evaluating policies to reduce peak-hour crowding.

script.description_zh: 明明車廂擠爆，為什麼大家還是搭同一班？一橋大學團隊用2015年日本搭車問卷中2740位西武新宿線通勤族的資料，對照時刻表找出每人搭的班次，再把大家的選擇當成互相影響的遊戲來反推。在主要估算裡，早到或遲到一分鐘的代價，約是滿載車廂多待一分鐘「額外」不適的10到12倍；不過這個倍數會隨到站時間的假設而大幅改變。
script.description_en: Why do commuters keep picking the most packed trains? Using survey answers from 2,740 commuters on Tokyo's Seibu Shinjuku Line matched to train timetables, researchers modeled train choice as a game where everyone's choice shapes crowding. In their main estimate, arriving a minute early or late weighed roughly ten to twelve times more than the extra discomfort of a minute on a full train, though that ratio depends heavily on assumptions about when people want to arrive.
script.method_summary: Fujishima and Matsumoto (Hitotsubashi University; Railway Technical Research Institute) study morning train choice on Tokyo's Seibu Shinjuku Line. Data: individual microdata from Japan's 2015 Public Transport Survey for Metropolitan Areas (MLIT): 2,740 commuter respondents, expanded to 140,473 commuters, boarding at 27 stations and heading to Takadanobaba/Seibu-Shinjuku (treated as one CBD). Each respondent's boarding/alighting stations and times were matched to the November 2015 timetable to infer the train used (89 trains up to 10:30 a.m., four service types). Desired CBD arrival times were built from reported work start times minus egress time minus an assumed 15-minute buffer (baseline common time 8:10). Each commuter's cost = travel time + crowding (linear in crowding rate, accumulated over segments) + early/late schedule delay. Because crowding depends on everyone's choices, train choice is modeled as a population potential game with logit revision; its closed-form stationary distribution gives a likelihood, approximated for large populations and maximized; standard errors come from a parametric bootstrap. Findings: all four costs positive; one minute early = 0.39 and late = 0.49 minutes of in-vehicle time, while one minute at 100% crowding adds only 0.04 minutes. Schedule delay dominates crowding across specifications, but the crowding parameter is sensitive to how desired arrival times are specified and is zero in some. Authors suggest flexible/staggered work hours alongside fare incentives.
script.limitations: Single line, one survey day in 2015, cross-sectional. Desired arrival times rely on an assumed 15-minute buffer and, in baseline, a common time; crowding cost is sensitive to this and reaches zero in some specifications. Train matching may contain errors (some implausible crowding rates). Linear crowding, no seated vs standing distinction; ignores limited expresses and transfers; assumes full information. Bootstrap ignores survey sampling uncertainty. No policy counterfactuals yet, so effects of discounts or flexible hours are not shown.

pick_reason: This paper uses observed train choices on a Tokyo commuter line and a population-game model to show how much commuters trade off delay, travel time and crowding. It is an everyday, non-AI behavior question that is computational and easy to show in steps: choices lead to crowding, which feeds back into choices, and the model recovers preferences from that loop. Signals: Notes suggest mixing in non-AI personal-stakes topics to break the run of AI-themed picks, and the strongest AI candidates sit too close to recent homework, AI-at-work and social-media-intervention episodes.

paper.title: Sanctions, Evasion, and Deterrence: Evidence from Speeding Enforcement
paper.abstract: The design of sanctions plays a central role in shaping reoffending behavior. We study the effects of fixed monetary fines and accumulating penalty points on speeding recidivism and liability transfer. Exploiting a large increase in sanctions in Queensland, Australia, we estimate the causal effects of these sanctions on subsequent offending and nomination of other drivers. Higher demerit points increase fine renomination, consistent with strategic blame shifting. Estimated reductions in reoffending are small among offenders facing higher fines alone. Reoffending falls by a substantial 4.6 percentage points when higher fines are accompanied by additional penalty points.

script.description_zh: 超速罰款大漲，大家就會少超速嗎？澳洲迪肯大學經濟學家比較昆士蘭2022年新規上路前後被測速照相拍到的駕駛，發現只加罰款的人再超速幾乎沒變，但罰款加駕照記點的那一級，一年內再犯明顯減少。同時，這一級的車主也更常把罰單轉給「別人開的車」。
script.description_en: Do bigger speeding fines make people slow down? Economists at Deakin University compared drivers caught by speed cameras just before and after Queensland's 2022 penalty hike. Higher fines alone barely changed repeat speeding, but where extra license points were added, repeat offenses dropped clearly, and owners also became more likely to name someone else as the driver.
script.method_summary: The authors use administrative data covering all camera-detected speeding offenses in Queensland, Australia (743,539 camera detections in 2022), linked by a unique driver ID. On 1 July 2022 Queensland raised fines in every speed band (e.g. 11-12 km/h over: AUD 183 to 431) but raised demerit points only for the 11-12 km/h band (1 to 3 points; 12 points in 3 years means license suspension). Using a regression discontinuity in time with a 150-day window, they compare offenders caught just before vs just after the reform. Recidivism (any new speeding offense within one year, excluding the first 14 days) is estimated on fixed cameras (149,755 offenses), which photograph from the front and showed balanced covariates and no transfer change. Liability transfer (owner nominating another driver) is studied on mobile cameras (438,590 offenses), which may shoot from behind. Findings: overall reoffending fell 1.6 percentage points (about 5%); for the 11-12 km/h band it fell 4.6 points (13%, from a 34.8% baseline); fine-only bands showed no clear effect. Transfer rates for mobile-camera 11-12 km/h fines rose about 30-60% relative to a low baseline (~1.6-2%), with no rise in other bands or for fixed cameras. Placebo tests in 2015-2019, bandwidth checks and a difference-in-differences comparison with 9-10 km/h offenders support the results.
script.limitations: Not a randomized experiment; identification relies on timing around one statewide reform. The 11-12 km/h band also had the largest fine increase, so points and fine size are only partly separated. The transfer discontinuity is not statistically significant at the preferred bandwidth (p=0.112) and is sensitive to bandwidth; event-study and DiD evidence is stronger. The data cannot distinguish truthful from untruthful nominations. Mobile-camera samples show compositional changes. Outcomes are detected reoffenses, not actual speeding or crashes, and results come from Queensland only.

pick_reason: The study uses a natural experiment, a big jump in speeding fines and penalty points in Queensland, to estimate on large administrative records whether harsher sanctions cut repeat offending or push drivers to shift the points onto someone else, which is a concrete everyday behavioural question with a clear causal design that fits in 3-4 visual steps. Signals: Channel notes suggest mixing in non-AI personal-stakes topics, since about 7 of the last 11 shorts were AI-themed, so among similar-quality candidates I favored this non-AI, money-and-rules paper over the AI-at-work and AI-persuasion options.

paper.title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
paper.abstract: Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

script.description_zh: 跟AI聊三輪，就能讓人對自己相信的陰謀論動搖。但到底是哪一招有效？卡內基美隆和康乃爾的研究團隊找了約2,200位美國人，把AI的說服方式一次拿掉一樣來測試。結果講明要說服、改成辯論、回答砍半都還有效，只有不准AI給證據時效果大減。
script.description_en: A short chat with AI can loosen people's grip on conspiracy theories, but why? Researchers from Carnegie Mellon and Cornell ran two experiments with about 2,200 Americans, removing one ingredient of the AI's approach at a time. Warning people, framing it as a debate, or halving the replies barely mattered; only banning evidence sharply weakened the effect.
script.method_summary: Two online experiments with U.S. adults (Study 1 N=1,290; Study 2 N=903; total 2,193). Participants described a conspiracy theory they found credible and why; an AI restated it and they rated their confidence 0-100. They then had a three-round live chat with GPT-4 (Study 1) or GPT-5.2 (Study 2) that countered their reasons, and rated again. Study 1 compared the original treatment (belief fell 80.5 to 69.6, about 10.9 points) with variants changing one feature: telling people the AI would persuade (9.1), debate framing (11.9), inform rather than persuade (11.6), roughly half-length replies (13.8), and two measurement changes; all were similar to baseline. Only 'No Facts', persuading without evidence or reasoning, sharply weakened it (3.8 points). Study 2 randomized original dialogue (14.6-point drop), a single tailored message (11.8, about 79% of the effect), and an unrelated-topic control chat (1.4). In Study 2, 23% of treated participants starting above the midpoint ended below it vs 1.5% in control. LLM-coded content analysis linked larger drops to facts/evidence and source citations, not rapport, stories, or empathy; persuaded participants mostly cited tailored facts and logic. Trust in AI modestly boosted effects but low-trust people still changed.
script.limitations: Participants were self-selected U.S. online volunteers, more educated and less religious than the population. Belief was measured immediately after the chat in these studies (durability comes from earlier work). Contrasts could only detect large differences, so smaller contributions from dialogue, rapport, or trust in AI cannot be ruled out. The No Facts prompt removed a bundle of features (facts, sources, precision), not one cleanly. The content and claim analyses are observational and coded by AI models, so they carry weaker causal warrant. Open-mindedness was measured after treatment.

pick_reason: Two large online experiments (N=2,193) take apart why personalized AI dialogues reduce conspiracy beliefs by removing possible causes one at a time, and find the debunking survives even when the AI's persuasive goal is disclosed. That gives a concrete, surprising misinformation result that fits a 3-4 step visual explanation. Signals: The notes suggest a lean toward everyday-AI and personal-stakes topics, and earlier AI-dialogue shorts like the deliberation one did above typical. This paper studies conspiracy beliefs rather than how people word political prompts, so it does not repeat the recent chatbot-politics episode.

paper.title: Retweeting patterns reveal partisan asymmetries in information sharing and signal state-level electoral outcomes in the 2020 US presidential election
paper.abstract: As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political ecosystems and relates to offline voting remains unclear. Here we reconstruct partisan information ecosystems from more than 500 million tweets generated during the 2020 US presidential election, integrating information diffusion across media outlets, influencers, and social peers. Contrary to the conventional expectation that broader information exposure promotes moderation, we find that retweeting a wider range of political information is associated with stronger political polarization. We further show systematic asymmetries in political information ecosystems: the Republican ecosystem is highly concentrated and ideologically biased, whereas the Democratic ecosystem is more dispersed and primarily organized around relatively moderate left-leaning sources. Finally, we demonstrate that several shared retweeting signatures robustly map onto state-level electoral outcomes despite cross-state heterogeneity. Our findings reveal asymmetric political information ecosystems as a key organizing principle of online political communication and identify collective retweeting patterns as a scalable signal of real-world voting behaviours.

script.description_zh: 多看對面的意見，真的會讓人變溫和嗎？研究團隊分析2020年美國大選期間超過五億則轉推，發現結果可能剛好相反。不過這只是相關，不能說是看了才改變。
script.description_en: Does seeing the other side make people more moderate? Researchers analyzed over half a billion retweets from the 2020 US election. Users who retweeted more cross-side media later moved further left if they were left-leaning, and further right if they were center or right. State-level patterns also matched election results, but these are associations, not proof of cause.
script.method_summary: The authors used a public list of tweet IDs collected with presidential candidates' names as search terms, covering December 2019 to February 2021. They retrieved about 543 million non-reply tweets (retweets and quote tweets) through the Twitter API. Each user's political leaning was scored from -3 (extreme left) to 3 (extreme right) by averaging the leaning of the news media they retweeted, using Media Bias/Fact Check ratings, with a parallel scoring for political figures. They then built a measure of 'ideological permeability': the average distance between a user's own leaning and the leaning of the media they retweeted, with extra weight for crossing to the opposite side. Splitting the timeline into six periods, they ran separate robust regressions asking whether higher permeability goes with later leftward or rightward shifts. Higher permeability went with later leftward shifts among Left and Left-Leaning users, and later rightward shifts among Center, Right-Leaning, Right and Extreme Right users. They also built co-exposure networks of media, politicians and user retweet communities, finding the Republican side more concentrated and the Democratic side more dispersed. At state level, the left-to-right user ratio, with a cutoff chosen on the same 50 states, classified Biden and Trump states with 92% accuracy (46 of 50), and a Lasso-based model of user-media retweeting patterns tracked vote margins, with out-of-bag R2 of 0.447.
script.limitations: The results are associations, not causal effects: the paper does not show that seeing opposing media causes people to shift. Twitter users are not representative of all voters, and user leaning is only approximated from the media they retweet. State location relies on self-reported profile data covering a small subset of users, the data are a sample of election-related tweets, and the state analysis uses only 38 states and a threshold chosen on the same data. The 46-of-50 figure is an in-sample classification, not a true forecast. It covers one platform and one election, so generalization is untested.

paper.title: Taste or Strategy? Nationalistic Bias and Competitor Penalties in Figure Skating Judging
paper.abstract: Many decisions rest on expert panels whose members have ties to some candidates, and favoritism is hard to tell from shared taste or better information. Using a rich dataset from figure skating, we find evidence of a strategic compatriot premium and a targeted penalty on the compatriot's close rivals. The premium falls along a randomly drawn start order and, before 2022/23, rises when close rivals have their own judges on the panel. The penalty grows with the compatriot's placement chances and fades once she is out of contention. A counterfactual analysis shows that these biases can shape close competitions.

script.description_zh: 花式滑冰裁判會給同國選手加分，還會小幅壓低她的近身對手嗎？兩位經濟學者分析十年、約二十萬筆裁判評分，發現抽籤決定的出場順序洩了底：加分會隨出場順序改變，不像單純的口味。研究也用模擬說明，這類偏差有可能影響很接近的比賽。
script.description_en: When a figure skating judge scores a compatriot higher, is it taste, familiarity, or strategy? Two economists used about 200,000 individual judge scores and randomly drawn start orders to tell them apart. The home-country boost changed with start order, and judges marked down their skater's close rivals. A simulation shows such bias could change close results.
script.method_summary: The authors built a dataset of 172 international figure skating competitions from 2016/17 to 2025/26: 23,254 performances by 2,470 skaters and 206,983 individual judge marks from 620 judges of 59 federations. Judge marks (execution, program components, and a synthetic total score) were converted to percent of a reference scale. Comparing judges on the same performance, with performance and judge fixed effects, a judge scored a skater from her own federation about 1.7 percent of the scale higher. Close rivals were defined by start order (within three starts), not by final placement, to avoid reverse causality. Judges marked rivals down by a small amount, mostly in second segments and mostly while the compatriot was still in contention. In first segments with a random open draw, the compatriot premium fell from about 1.99 for the first starter to 1.29 for the last, so at least about a fifth of the average premium cannot be explained by fixed taste or familiarity. Before 2022/23, the premium rose when more of the compatriot's later rivals had their own judge on the panel. Finally, the authors redrew admissible Milan 2026 Olympic panels and rescored performances: the ice dance title changed hands in 45 to 57 percent of redraws and the women's title in 20 to 27 percent. The trimmed mean removes only a small part of such bias.
script.limitations: The study is observational and cannot see judges' intentions; strategic scoring is inferred from patterns. Rivals are defined by start order, which measures true rivalry with noise. The evidence that the premium rises with rivals' judges appears only before 2022/23 and not in the later era. Several interaction estimates carry non-trivial negative weights. Judge-specific estimates are unstable, so the paper warns against using them to accuse individual judges. The counterfactual does not question official Olympic results, and the setting is only figure skating.

paper.title: Where Language-Model Vocabulary Rose on Stack Exchange
paper.abstract: Stack Overflow banned answers generated by ChatGPT five days after the model's release, and many other Stack Exchange sites announced similar rules. I measure the vocabulary of the answers posted afterwards, 3.8 million answers on 170 sites from 2019 to 2024. A fixed list of 56 words that language models overuse rose about 14 percent above its pre-2023 trend, while the highest of 1,000 frequency-matched lists of ordinary words rose about 7 percent. In a screen of 15 site traits measured before the release, the strongest predictor of where the rise happened was the share of answers that received a body edit within 30 days of posting. On the least edited third of sites the list rose about 29 percent relative to matched controls, and on the most edited third it did not change. The gradient is also present among answers that were never edited. It follows the share of answers edited by their own authors, and the share edited by others adds little once that share is held fixed. Use of the model is unobserved, so these results cannot separate lower use on sites with a high self-edit share from any effect of editing on what the vocabulary records. Any vocabulary-based estimate for the network as a whole therefore pools sites where the marker vocabulary rose sharply with sites where it did not change.
