script.description_zh: 研究團隊分析 170 個問答網站、380 萬則回答，發現 AI 愛用字整體變多。編輯最少的三分之一網站增加約 29%，編輯最多的三分之一則沒變。研究看不到誰真的用了 ChatGPT，所以原因還不清楚。
script.description_en: Did the words AI chatbots overuse rise in Stack Exchange answers after ChatGPT? A study of 3.8 million answers on 170 sites found about a 14% rise overall, but it varied a lot: about 29% on the least-edited third of sites and no change on the most-edited third. Actual ChatGPT use was not observed, so the cause is unclear.
script.method_summary: The study uses the April 2024 Stack Exchange data dump: 170 sites and about 3.83 million answers from January 2019 to March 2024. Stack Overflow and meta sites were excluded. Code, HTML and URLs were stripped to keep prose. The outcome is a fixed list of 56 words that earlier studies found language models overuse (for example delve, crucial, ensure, furthermore), set before the author read any Stack Exchange text. The author measured how often answers contain these words and compared the rise after ChatGPT's release against each site's own pre-2023 trend. To check general drift, the author built 1,000 control lists of ordinary words matched on frequency. The marker list rose about 14 percent above trend, while the highest control list rose about 7 percent. Two lists of formal words (connectives and formal adjectives/adverbs) were also checked: with equal site weights both ended 3 to 6 percent below trend, though with answer weighting the connectives rose up to 10 percent. The author then screened 15 site traits measured before the release to see where the rise happened. The strongest predictor was the share of answers receiving a body edit within 30 days of posting. On the least edited third of sites the list rose about 29 percent relative to matched controls, and on the most edited third it did not change. The gradient also appears among never-edited answers and follows the share of answers edited by their own authors; edits by others add little once that is held fixed.
script.limitations: Use of ChatGPT is not observed, so the study cannot tell whether sites with many self-edits used the model less or whether editing habits changed what the vocabulary records. The edit-share analysis was not planned; it emerged from a screen of 15 traits and needs replication. The study does not code which sites banned generated answers or when, so it says nothing about what the rules did. Much of the pattern rests on the word ensure, and the word list was built from scientific text.

paper.title: The Rebundling of Freelance Work in the AI Age
paper.abstract: This paper examines how freelance work is changing in the AI era. We compare the activities people undertake in ChatGPT with the work clients request on Upwork, an online freelance platform, and examine how clients combine tasks into projects. We find that activities more prevalent in ChatGPT tend to lose marketplace share on Upwork, while those less prevalent tend to gain share. Within AI-related work, demand is becoming more diverse, and job postings combine tasks that were rarely requested together before the generative AI era. AI-related postings also have substantially larger project budgets and involve more hours of work, while differences in hourly rates are small. Together, these findings suggest that AI is reshaping not only which tasks clients outsource, but also how they combine tasks into larger, higher-value projects.

script.description_en: How is freelance work changing in the AI era? This OpenAI and Upwork preprint compares what people do in ChatGPT with what clients hire for on Upwork. AI-related jobs combine more unusual task pairs and carry bigger budgets. The findings are descriptive and do not prove AI caused them.
script.method_summary: The study combines two datasets. First, about 36,900 sampled ChatGPT conversations (consumer accounts, January 2025 to June 2026) were each assigned by a classifier to one of Upwork's work subcategories, excluding schoolwork and unclear conversations. Second, Upwork Marketplace job postings were classified as AI-related or not by an LLM-based pipeline. The authors defined ChatGPT intensity for each of 63 matched subcategories as its share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 relative to its share of Upwork postings in H1 2023, and compared it with how its share of postings changed. About 68 percent of subcategories either had higher ChatGPT intensity and lost share or lower intensity and gained share. Next, more than 3,000 activity descriptions were grouped into 400+ standardized tasks, and each posting's bundle is its distinct tasks. AI-related postings averaged 3.35 distinct tasks versus 3.19 for other postings. Task pairs seen in fewer than 200 pre-generative-AI postings were called historically uncommon; they made up 8.4 percent of pairs in AI-related jobs versus 2.4 percent in other jobs. Even among jobs of similar size, subcategory and month, AI-related jobs combined tasks with lower historical prevalence. Fixed-price budgets were about 52 percent higher after controls, hourly rates only about 1.5 percent higher, and hours worked in the first 90 days of hired hourly contracts about 41 percent higher.
script.limitations: The ChatGPT and Upwork datasets are not directly matched, and neither represents the whole labor market. All comparisons are descriptive associations and do not identify causal effects of AI or of ChatGPT use on freelance demand. Classification of AI-related jobs and tasks relies on LLM-based pipelines. Budgets and rates are posted prices, not final payments. The task analysis covers only an early phase of generative AI adoption, through 2025.

script.description_en: Does trust in the CDC predict who wore masks and got vaccinated? This PNAS study analyzed 20 rounds of a US national survey and found trust gaps larger than those by age, income, education or party. It shows an association, not proof of cause.
script.method_summary: The authors used 20 waves of CHIP50, a nationally representative nonprobability online survey of US adults run roughly every one to two months from April 2020 to January 2024, weighted to Census benchmarks. Respondents rated trust in the CDC, doctors and hospitals, state governments and banks on a four-point scale (a lot to not at all). Outcomes were self-reported protective behaviors: always wearing a mask, always avoiding contact, always avoiding crowds, frequent handwashing, plus vaccination and visiting a doctor or hospital. Unadjusted, the mask-wearing gap between highest and lowest CDC trust averaged 38.8 percentage points, versus 25.9 for Democrats vs. Republicans and about 6 to 10 for age, education and income. Survey-weighted logistic regressions adjusted for age, race, education, income, urbanicity, party, ideology, region and employment; the adjusted mask gap stayed around 32 to 37 points in landmark waves. Adding blocks of covariates step by step showed only political identity noticeably shrank the trust gap (about 41 to 31 points). Removing trust hurt model fit more than removing any other block. Trust in banks, used as a negative control, showed a much smaller gap (about 3 to 6 points), and trust in the CDC was unrelated to doctor visits. The authors propose splitting epidemic models into high, medium and low trust groups with different contact and vaccination rates.
script.limitations: The results are observational associations, not causal effects; political identity may be a mediator or competing factor rather than a simple confounder. Behaviors are self-reported. Trust was measured with a single survey item. The parallel decline of trust and protective behavior cannot be separated from pandemic fatigue. CHIP50 is a nonprobability US sample, so low-trust people may be underrepresented. The proposed trust-based transmission model is a framework and was not tested against epidemic data.

paper.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour
paper.abstract: People increasingly ask AI chatbots for advice, yet large language models (LLMs) are sycophantic, overconfident, and can amplify human cognitive biases. In this article, we investigate how people perceive advice from humans versus LLMs and whether AI advice reshapes incentive-compatible donation decisions. Using Carrier, a new experimental platform, we designed an experiment where participants made a donation decision after discussing it with an AI chatbot advisor, another human, or receiving no advice. Participants judged LLM advisors to be significantly more rational, trustworthy, convincing, and sycophantic than human advisors. Analysis of chatlogs showed that LLMs were more engaged than human advisors: they shared more facts and more often stated their opinion and justified their recommendations. Despite this, donation decisions did not vary across conditions.

script.description_en: More and more people ask AI chatbots for advice. In this study, about 420 decision-makers chose how much of a £97 lottery prize to donate to a malaria charity, after chatting with ChatGPT, chatting with a person, or getting no advice (about 150 other participants acted as the human advisors). People rated ChatGPT as more rational and trustworthy, yet final donations showed no clear difference across groups, though the evidence for no difference was only weak to moderate.
script.method_summary: The study ran on an online platform called Carrier with participants recruited via Prolific (600 recruited, 572 analysed, which includes about 149 human advisors; roughly 423 were decision-makers, 150 recruited per condition). Decision-makers entered a lottery for £97 and decided how much to keep versus donate to the Against Malaria Foundation; if they won, their decision was executed with real money. Human advisors only gave advice and made a hypothetical donation decision. Decision-makers were randomly assigned to discuss the decision in a live text chat with an LLM (ChatGPT), with another participant acting as advisor, or with no one. Everyone was told truthfully who they would chat with. Advice-condition participants stated an initial non-binding preference before chatting and then made a final decision. Afterwards they rated advisors on rationality, trustworthiness, convincingness and sycophancy. Chat transcripts were coded by another LLM, validated against a research assistant on 10% of chats. Average final donations were £25.8 (LLM advice), £28.3 (human advice) and £30.4 (no advice), with no significant differences and only weak to moderate Bayesian evidence for the null. Participants rated the LLM as more rational, trustworthy, convincing and sycophantic. LLM advisors wrote far more, shared more facts and reasons, and in 87% of chats explicitly or implicitly affirmed the advisee's action versus 47% for humans (coded per conversation). Where advisors named an amount (about 33% of human chats, 64% of LLM chats), suggestions were nearly identical (about £36.7 vs £35.9); the authors offer this as one possible explanation for the null result, not a tested cause.
script.limitations: The study tested a single, one-off donation decision to one charity in a short chat of about four to five minutes, with online Prolific participants. The no-difference result rests on weak to moderate Bayesian evidence for the null, so it does not prove advice never matters. The similar suggested amounts are only a possible explanation, not tested as the cause, and amounts were named in only some chats. Only about 64% of advisees in the human condition believed they chatted with a human. Chat coding relied on an LLM autograder, and the paper is a preprint.

paper.title: Food co-purchasing networks encode geographic disparities in cardiometabolic health
paper.abstract: Unhealthy diets are a major driver of cardiometabolic disease, yet the geospatial structure of dietary behavior and its links to population health remain poorly understood. While large-scale retail transaction data offer a unique view of population dietary behavior, conventional approaches reduce purchases to isolated items, not accounting for how foods are actually combined. Here, we analyze 51 million grocery receipts across 95 Danish municipalities using a statistically validated bipartite network framework to isolate co-purchases that product popularity alone cannot explain. We find that, although municipalities buy largely the same products, their co-purchasing networks reorganize along a continuous urban-to-peripheral gradient in how those products are combined. The network backbone can be resolved into modular dietary communities whose local cohesion allows us to predict cardiometabolic prescriptions, explaining a quarter to a half of the variance left after sociodemographic adjustment, beyond what product prevalence alone accounts for. Ultra-processed foods (UPFs) show no spatial gradient in prevalence and are located at the network periphery, where they share baskets with fresh foods but rarely form the combinations that hold the network together. Taken together, our findings show that geographic dietary differences are encoded not only in what people purchase, but in how foods are systematically combined within shopping baskets, offering a scalable network approach for population nutritional epidemiology.

script.description_zh: 丹麥研究團隊分析五千一百萬張超市收據，發現各地買的東西差不多，食物的搭配方式卻不一樣。各地搭配得多緊密，能幫忙猜當地的處方率，不過這只是相關，不代表搭配造成疾病。
script.description_en: Danish towns buy nearly the same groceries, but combine them differently. Researchers analyzed 51 million receipts and found that how tightly foods are combined tracks local prescription rates. It is an area-level link, not proof that combinations cause disease.
script.method_summary: The researchers analyzed 51 million point-of-sale receipts from 553 Netto supermarkets (Salling Group) across 95 of Denmark's 98 municipalities, collected over about 79 days in early 2025. Non-food items were removed and edible items were grouped into 3,405 products, which were matched to the Danish food-composition database and given processing scores. Receipts were treated as baskets, and a statistical null model that preserves basket sizes and product popularity was used to keep only product pairs bought together more often than chance. This was done for each municipality and for a national network. Municipal networks differed along an urban-to-peripheral gradient: four big cities clustered together, and far-away towns combined foods differently despite largely shared catalogs, e.g. vegetable-cheese pairs shrank to about 28% of the urban-core share. The national network split into 12 communities. How cohesively each community was co-purchased locally predicted 2024 prescription rates for diabetes, cardiovascular and lipid medicines beyond sociodemographics, and a version that removes product prevalence added about a quarter to nearly half of the remaining variance. Ultra-processed foods had no geographic gradient in purchase share and sat at the network periphery everywhere.
script.limitations: Receipts show what households buy at one chain, not what each person eats, and miss food bought elsewhere or wasted. The design is cross-sectional and correlational, so it cannot show that food combinations cause cardiometabolic disease. Purchases and prescriptions are aggregated by municipality and not linked at the individual level, so the shoppers need not be the people filling prescriptions. Prescription rates are proxies for treated disease. Physical activity and other confounders are not measured. Purchases cover about three months in 2025, while health data are from 2024.

paper.title: Hi Gemini, Who Should I Vote For? The Benefits (and Problems) of Using LLMs As Voting Advice Applications
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores how well off-the-shelf LLMs function as voting advice applications (VAAs). In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM's advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM's recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at approximately 1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM's recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

script.description_zh: 如果請AI幫你決定投哪個政黨，會怎麼樣？義大利LUISS大學的研究團隊，拿六千多位德國選民在稅收、移民、氣候的立場，請Gemini推薦政黨。結果超過一半的人會換到更貼近自己立場的政黨，但Gemini明顯偏推AfD，而且推薦的理由很難追查。
script.description_en: Would an AI chatbot give good voting advice? This study fed Gemini 3 Flash the views of over 6,000 German voters on taxes, immigration, and climate, and asked it to pick a party for each. For over half, the pick matched their views better than their actual vote, but Gemini favored the AfD and almost never picked Die Linke.
script.method_summary: The authors tested whether an off-the-shelf large language model, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, can work like a voting advice application. They used the post-election 2025 German Longitudinal Election Study, restricted to 6,022 respondents who reported voting. Each respondent gave a position on a 1-11 scale and an importance rating on a 1-5 scale for three issues: taxes versus social services, immigration, and climate change versus economic growth. Respondents were sent to the LLM in 354 batches of 20, with only these answers (no demographics or party identification), and the LLM named one party for each person's party vote. Congruence was the importance-weighted distance between a voter and a party, using party positions from the 2024 Chapel Hill expert survey. The LLM's pick was compared with the party the respondent actually voted for and with an Expert model, a salience-weighted proximity model that picks the closest party. For just over 50% of respondents the LLM pick was more congruent than their actual vote, for just over a third it was the same, and for just over 12% it was worse. The LLM matched the Expert model for just under 70%. Gemini recommended the AfD to 29% (Expert model about 19-20%, actual vote about 15%) and Die Linke to under 2% (Expert model 5%). Gains were larger for people with low political interest (43% higher predicted gain) and low education (32% higher). A repeat run gave the same party in 85% of cases.
script.limitations: The study covers only three issues, so it cannot show that following the LLM's advice would make voters better off overall. It tests one model, Gemini 3 Flash, with respondents processed in batches of 20, and uses a structured numeric input unlike real chats. Congruence relies on expert party ratings, not the parties' actual platforms, and some respondents may have underreported voting AfD. The authors cannot explain why the biases occur, and it is untested whether people would follow the advice or whether other LLMs behave the same.

paper.title: Asymmetric rhetorical strategies drive partisanship in television news
paper.abstract: Television remains a dominant source of political information in the United States, yet systematic evidence on how partisanship is expressed in televised news remains limited. Prior research has largely treated partisanship as a one-dimensional construct, offering limited insight into the rhetorical strategies that underlie ideological bias. Here, by analyzing over 400,000 news episodes using large language models (LLMs), we provide a multi-dimensional measure of partisanship bias in television news across six major U.S. news stations (2013--2025). We identify eight interpretable linguistic features that explain 73% of partisanship variance in television news.\ Our findings reveal systematic asymmetries across stations. While MSNBC and CNN shifted leftward during Republican presidencies and moderated under Democratic presidencies, Fox News increased its conservative alignment following each election regardless of the electoral outcome. Beyond aggregate trends, MSNBC and CNN emphasized attacks on Republican actors more than reinforcement of Democratic positions, whereas Fox News reinforced Republican viewpoints substantially more than it attacked Democratic viewpoints. The association between in-group praise and out-group attacks was also threefold stronger on Fox News than on MSNBC. These results are validated against trained human raters and replicated with four additional LLMs with differing political leanings. Together, our study reveals systematic station-level differences in the rhetorical strategies with which ideological slant is communicated in television news, opening new opportunities for future research on media effects, audience attitudes, and political communication.

script.description_en: Are Fox News and MSNBC mirror images? A study used AI to read over 400,000 US TV news episodes from 2013 to 2025. Fox leaned on praising its own side, while MSNBC and CNN leaned on attacking the other side. The analysis shows correlation, not cause.
script.method_summary: The authors analyzed 408,464 US television news episodes (3,505,401 segments of about 800 words, roughly five minutes each) from Fox News, MSNBC, CNN, ABC, CBS and NBC, January 2013 to March 2025. GPT-4o was prompted to give each segment a partisanship score from 0 (strongly liberal) to 100 (strongly conservative) plus a short explanation. It scored a stratified sample of 10,000 episodes (86,131 segments); a neural network trained on those labels then scored the rest. The scores agreed strongly with three trained human raters on 250 segments (r = 0.92), about as well as the raters agreed with each other. From reading the explanations, the authors defined eight features: negative sentiment toward Democrats or Republicans, reinforcing each party's viewpoints, blaming each party, inflammatory language, and fact-based reporting. A linear regression with these eight binary labels explained 73% of held-out variance in partisanship scores. Fox reinforced Republican views in 69.8% of segments versus 61.6% with negative sentiment toward Democrats, whereas MSNBC (52.5% vs 39.3%) and CNN (35.0% vs 22.7%) attacked Republicans more than they reinforced Democratic views. Fox moved more conservative after every election, while MSNBC and CNN moved with presidential incumbency. Fox paired praise and attacks about three times more strongly than MSNBC. Broadcast networks stayed near neutral. Results replicated with four other LLMs.
script.limitations: The analysis is correlational and cannot say why stations changed or how audiences are affected. All scores and rhetorical labels come from LLMs (then a neural network copying them), validated on small human-coded samples. The eight features leave about 27% of the variance unexplained. Only three months of the second Trump presidency are included, so conclusions about that period are weak. Transcripts come from closed captions, and broadcast data come from New York affiliates.

paper.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
paper.abstract: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

script.description_en: When you pick a news story, do you go by politics, rank, or likes? A Spanish team had 370 Americans click one story from ten headlines, with story order and like counts assigned at random. Stories showing more likes got clicked more, and likes alone predicted clicks better than rank or stance alone.
script.method_summary: The study, by researchers at Universitat Pompeu Fabra, uses a conditional multinomial logit model, a standard discrete choice model, to describe which of 10 news articles a person clicks. The utility of each article combines three features: the match between the user's and the article's political stance (five-point scale from extreme left to extreme right), the article's rank position, and the log of its displayed engagement count (likes and shares). Data come from two online experiments with US participants recruited through Prolific: E1 (March 2026, 166 participants) with no engagement counts shown, and E2 (September 2026, 204 participants) with likes and shares shown. Each participant did four tasks, one each on climate change, immigration, gender policies and vaccination, choosing one article from a scrollable list of 10 (two per stance category). Article positions were randomized per participant and topic; in E2 like and share counts were randomly assigned to articles, independent of position. Likelihood-ratio tests showed that adding engagement improved fit on every topic. In 10 repetitions of 10-fold cross-validation on E2, engagement alone predicted held-out clicks better than stance alone or rank alone, and the full model did best. Observed clicks: top-ranked articles 17.8% vs bottom-ranked 7.8%; highest like counts 21% vs lowest 7.2%. Model counterfactuals suggest moving an article from bottom to top more than doubles its click probability, and swapping lowest for highest engagement roughly triples it.
script.limitations: The two conditions (without and with engagement cues) were run six months apart and participants were not randomly assigned between them, so the samples may differ. The causal evidence for engagement comes from the randomized counts within E2 and concerns the displayed size of the counts, not the effect of making engagement cues visible. The participants were US online panelists making one-time choices in an experiment, so it is unknown whether the effects hold in real browsing, or what they mean for news diversity or polarization.}</br>

paper.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
paper.abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

script.description_zh: 史丹佛團隊找了625位每天用ChatGPT的美國人，抽籤讓一組停用一天、一組停用兩週。停兩週的人覺得比較不孤單，面對面見的人也變多。不過差距不大，資料也是自己填的，原因還不能確定。
script.description_en: What happens if you quit ChatGPT for two weeks? A randomized experiment with 625 US ChatGPT users compared one day without AI against two weeks. The two-week group felt less lonely and reported more in-person interaction, but mood did not clearly change and the reasons remain suggestive.
script.method_summary: The researchers ran a preregistered randomized deactivation experiment with 625 US-based, active ChatGPT users recruited through Prolific. They had to use ChatGPT at least 15 minutes a day and have had an account for at least a month, and were paid to abstain. Participants were randomly assigned to abstain from AI assistants for 14 days (treatment, 306 people) or one day (control, 319 people). A Chrome browser extension blocked 36 AI assistant sites and checked compliance. Participants completed a baseline survey, interim, midline and endline surveys, daily short check-ins about their emotions, number of people they interacted with, time socializing and time working, and a follow-up two weeks after the study ended. Using linear mixed-effects models, two weeks of deactivation reduced loneliness relative to control (about 0.1 standard deviations) and increased social support and the number of in-person interactions. Daily reports showed more social interactions in the treatment group. Loneliness stayed lower at the two-week follow-up. There was no significant change in emotional state, overall well-being or time spent working. Open-ended answers suggested people turned to others for help they would have asked AI for. Exploratory mediation analysis suggested more socializing and social satisfaction may help explain the loneliness drop. Longer-time ChatGPT users showed larger loneliness reductions.
script.limitations: Outcomes were mostly self-reported, and participants were paid US ChatGPT users from an online panel, so results may not generalize. Fewer control participants than treatment participants finished the study, and about 19% of treatment completers did not fully comply. The loneliness effect was small, and mood and overall well-being did not change significantly. The mediation analysis was exploratory, so the paper cannot prove that more socializing caused the drop in loneliness. Only two weeks were studied, and OpenAI funded participant payments (it had no role in the study design or analysis).

paper.title: The Times They Are A-Changin': Tracking Global Trends through the Lens of Web Search
paper.abstract: Human societies have always left traces of their collective priorities, from cave drawings and stone carvings to chronicles on papyrus and printed books. In the digital era, these traces increasingly emerge through social media footprints and web search behavior at a global scale. We construct the first large-scale longitudinal dataset of Google Year in Search trends, spanning 15 years, to characterize how collective public attention evolves across countries and time. Because search engines like Google and Bing do not publicly release raw search logs, Year in Search provides a rare cross-national archive of annually salient search interests. The dataset is supplemented with a manually curated, unified ten-category semantic taxonomy with strong inter-annotator agreement. We focus on four categories (Information Seeking, Personality, Entertainment, and Sports) to investigate how collective attention varies across geographic and socio-cultural contexts. Our analyses reveal a consistently glocalized structure of collective attention: countries converge strongly in profession-level personality attention while remaining differentiated in the specific individuals they search for, yet profession-level similarity is only weakly associated with geographic region and income group. Information seeking is globally dominated by politics and health, while regional distributions show varying degrees of divergence. Crisis periods are associated with both shared and regionally differentiated shifts. Entertainment and sports attention likewise combine globally prominent interests with regional differentiation. Overall, our findings suggest that web search data provide a valuable computational lens for observing collective attention at scale, acting as a living archive of how societal priorities vary across countries and change over time.

script.description_en: Do people everywhere search for the same celebrities? Researchers gathered Google's yearly top-search lists for many countries from 2011 to 2025, tagged each searched person's profession, and compared countries pair by pair. Countries searched for similar kinds of people, but almost never the same individuals.
script.method_summary: The authors built a longitudinal dataset from Google's Year in Search pages, which list the most prominent trending search topics for each country each year. They collected the country pages in January 2025, translated non-English entries into English, and kept 2011-2025 for countries with at least 12 years of data, averaging 52 countries per year and 6,772 trending topic entries. Three annotators sorted topic labels into ten categories (Cohen's kappa about 0.83). For the personality category, three annotators looked up each searched person and tagged a profession (Fleiss's kappa 0.79). To test glocalization, they computed, for every year and every pair of countries, the Jaccard overlap between the two countries' sets of professions and between their sets of individual names. Profession overlap averaged 0.47 (range 0.41 to 0.53) with no clear trend, while name overlap averaged 0.04. Countries were also clustered by profession profile; pairs in the same region or income group were only slightly more similar than pairs across them. Some distant, differently-wealthy pairs, such as Belgium and Malaysia, were very similar. The paper also covers information seeking, entertainment and sports.
script.limitations: The data are Google's curated yearly summaries of salient searches, not complete search logs, so the paper shows relative attention rather than search volumes or individual behavior. Coverage depends on Google's publication: countries such as China and Russia are missing, and data exist only at the country level. Annotation was done by people and translation by machine. The paper shows associations only; it does not explain why countries share job types but not names.

paper.title: Physical co-presence of workers is linked with the evolution of interfirm networks
paper.abstract: Inter-firm transaction networks underpin modern economies and are critical for economic growth and resilience. Previous studies have largely explained the formation of inter-firm ties through spatial proximity. Yet people routinely move across space, creating opportunities for encounters that extend beyond geographical proximity. How these opportunities relate to inter-firm transaction relationships remains poorly understood. Here, we combine large-scale mobile phone mobility data with a multi-year panel of transactions among 196,317 firms in Tokyo to quantify encounter opportunities between workers and examine their association with inter-firm transaction ties. We find that pairs of areas with greater opportunities for encounters one another are more likely to have transaction links and new link formation between previously unconnected firms. This association is particularly pronounced in information- and service-intensive industries, reflecting the importance of encounter opportunities for exchange involving intangible knowledge and service. Indirect connections through shared neighbors in the encounter network are also positively associated with subsequent transaction formation across industries, but not within industries. These findings suggest that urban policies shaping connectivity formed through human mobility could play a significant role in the development and resilience of economic networks.

script.description_en: Which Tokyo firms end up trading with each other? Researchers used phone location data from about 330,000 people to measure how often workers from different areas are in the same place at the same time, then compared that with firm transaction records. Areas whose workers met more were more likely to trade, though this shows a link, not a cause.
script.method_summary: The study combines anonymized smartphone GPS data (329,149 users observed in Tokyo, July to September 2019, about 3.5% of working-age residents) with Teikoku Databank records of buyer-supplier relationships among 196,317 Tokyo-headquartered firms from 2016 to 2022. Firm headquarters were mapped to small hexagonal cells (about 76 m edge length). Workers were identified as users who spent at least 5 hours on a weekday in one firm cell on at least 40 days across at least 12 weeks. For each pair of cells, the authors computed a meeting probability: the chance that a random worker from one cell and one from the other were in the same place in the same 30-minute window, normalized by how often both groups were active at the same time. Logistic regressions with cell fixed effects and controls related this to whether a transaction link existed and whether a new link formed later. A doubling of meeting probability was associated with about 1.4% higher odds of a link existing and about 1.9% higher odds of new link formation. A gravity benchmark based on distance and worker counts did not reproduce the association, and shifting trajectories to other dates cut the coefficient by about 79%. The association was concentrated in working-hour encounters and was strongest for information, finance and professional services pairs. No consistent association with link dissolution was found.
script.limitations: The analysis is observational, so it cannot show that encounters cause transactions; existing relationships may generate travel, and stable features of area pairs may drive both. Co-presence measures only an opportunity to meet, not an actual conversation, and mobility is aggregated to workplace cells, so it is unknown whether the people are employed by the transacting firms. Mobility covers only three months of 2019, later transactions span COVID-19, transaction data mainly record major partners at headquarters level, and the study covers only Tokyo.

paper.title: Political Orientation and Participation in Prediction Markets: Large Stakes Converge, Small Stakes Diverge
paper.abstract: Prediction markets offer a way to study collective expectations and beliefs: people express their views on various events and, by putting money behind their predictions, take on the risks of their judgments. As a result, the scale of investment can reveal additional dimensions of individual behavior and beliefs. In this study, we use a complex network approach to examine the structure of user participation, drawing on roughly 1.14 billion transaction records from the Polymarket platform, covering more than 3.1 million wallet addresses and 764,000 prediction events. To do this, we build a bipartite network of users and events and analyze patterns of investment concentration, connections between topics, and the network's community structure. Our findings show a highly skewed distribution of financial participation: 1\% of events account for 64\% of total transaction volume, while 1\% of wallets account for 79.2\% of total financial participation. We also examine how investment scale and political orientation shape user participation patterns. Focusing on the 2024 U.S. presidential election, we compare users who invested exclusively in a Trump victory or exclusively in a Harris victory, grouping wallets by purchase size rather than by retail or institutional status. The results show that among large-scale investors, capital allocation patterns across topics are more similar between the two political groups; in contrast, these patterns diverge more and vary more among small-scale investors. This result holds across six different ways of representing and comparing the networks, and four of these differences are also statistically supported.

script.description_zh: 2024年美國大選，有人只押賀錦麗，有人只押川普。研究團隊用Polymarket約11.4億筆交易，比較兩邊九月下注金額最大和最小5%的人，十月在其他題目上的押法。結果大額組的兩邊比較像，但只有四種比法通過統計檢驗，原因也還不清楚。
script.description_en: How do people who bet on Trump and people who bet on Harris spread their other bets? A study of about 1.14 billion trades on Polymarket found that the biggest-stake groups on the two sides allocated money more alike than the smallest-stake groups. All six comparisons pointed the same way, but only four were statistically supported. It compares groups over one month, so it cannot show individual views, causes or political bias. Paper: Hosseinzadeh, Hosseiny and Jafari, arXiv 2026.
script.method_summary: The authors used about 1.14 billion executed trades (roughly 41.3 billion USDC) from the Polymarket prediction market, covering over 3.1 million wallet addresses and about 764,000 events. They built a bipartite network linking wallets to events, weighted by traded amount, and measured concentration: the top 1% of events hold 64% of volume and the top 1% of wallets hold 79.2% of participation. Community detection on the whole network found 149 communities in the amount-weighted version. For the election case study, they took September 2024 YES purchases in the presidential winner market. Purchase-size cutoffs were computed across one pool of all 21,301 buyers of either candidate (including 4,466 who bought both): Top 5% means at least about 2,788 USDC and Bottom 5% at most about 1.09 USDC. Only afterwards were Harris-only and Trump-only cohorts selected within each tier. They then measured how each cohort spread its October trading across 22 subjects outside the election, and compared Harris and Trump cohorts using Jensen-Shannon divergence (a measure of how different two distributions are). The Top pair was closer than the Bottom pair (0.243 vs 0.457 bits for amount-edge networks) and closer in all six representations. Four of the six contrasts were supported by a label-randomization test after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.0006), while amount profiles (p = 0.3274) and amount edges (p = 0.3357) were not; in the amount-edge view, HB-TT was closer than HT-TT.
script.limitations: The comparison is between aggregate cohorts, not individual wallets, and wallets need not be distinct people. An election purchase does not establish political affiliation, wealth or motive, so the gap cannot be attributed to political bias, better information or stake size as a cause. Only two tiers (top and bottom 5%) were compared, so no graded trend with stake size is shown. Only October activity was examined, with unequal active fractions and small cohorts (135 to 360 active wallets), on one platform and one election. Two of six comparisons were not statistically supported. The study is observational.

paper.title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
paper.abstract: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.

script.description_en: "I liked them before they were cool": do early fans really leave once an artist blows up? Researchers analyzed the listening logs of about 600,000 Last.fm users and found 78 sudden surges with no new album. They compared early fans with those of similar artists. Fewer early fans stopped listening and more lapsed fans came back, though the study only sees plays, not feelings.
script.method_summary: The study used MLHD+, a cleaned release of Last.fm listening histories: about 594,415 users and 21.1 billion time-stamped plays from 2005 to 2013, linked to MusicBrainz so each artist is recognised however its name is spelled. Last.fm records every play and shows it on the user's profile by default. Study 1 detected 78 'crowd arrivals': months between 2007 and mid-2012 when an artist's newcomers tripled compared with the previous year, the artist had an existing audience, and MusicBrainz showed no new release around the event (for example after a song was used in a film or TV series). Early fans were users who had played the artist at least ten times in months -24 to -7 before the event and were regular Last.fm users. Each treated artist was compared with up to five artists with no surge, matched on time since their latest studio album. Among early fans still listening before the event, 25.8% stopped playing the artist in the next six months versus 29.1% for comparison fans; among lapsed fans, 29.6% returned versus 25.0%. No such gaps existed one window earlier. Fans who kept listening gave the song most newcomers played a 3.0 percentage point larger share of their plays (from 8.4%), with no shift to deep cuts. Returning rose more after larger surges, and fans with niche tastes or facing more mainstream crowds did not quit more. Study 2 compared Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with losing nominees and found few new listeners and no clear change.
script.limitations: The data come from Last.fm users between 2005 and 2013, committed music enthusiasts who logged their listening, and only plays matched to MusicBrainz recordings. Crowd arrivals were not randomly assigned, so the comparison does not prove cause. The study observes what people played, not how they felt or what they chose to display or say, so identity effects in deliberate displays remain untested. Many events had other recordings near the date. The award study had few events and showed no clear result. Results may not hold on today's algorithm-driven streaming services.

paper.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
paper.abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

script.description_en: What do proverbs actually tell us to do? Researchers merged seven English proverb dictionaries into nearly 50,000 proverbs, had an AI read each one, and checked it against human raters. Most proverbs give advice, favoring caution, the long term, honesty and kindness, but they split on autonomy versus compliance. Paper: Lejarraga, Wulff & Hertwig, arXiv 2026.
script.method_summary: The authors compiled 49,528 unique proverbs from seven published dictionaries (five mostly American or British, two multicultural or global). They used the open model Gemma-3-27B to write a short gist for each proverb, assign up to three topic tags, and rate it on five-point scales: whether it gives guidance on how to act (prescriptive), and which pole it favors on nine dimensions: risk vs caution, short vs long term, own vs others' interests, autonomy vs compliance, trust vs suspicion, honesty vs deception, equality vs hierarchy, kindness vs malice, cooperation vs competition. For validation, two trained research assistants rated a random sample of 500 proverbs, with and without the gist. The model agreed more with the average human rating than the humans agreed with each other on every dimension. The model rated 67.1% of proverbs as prescriptive (humans 73.8%). Among prescriptive proverbs, both model and humans found a clear lean toward caution, long-term outcomes, honesty and kindness, and a moderate lean toward suspicion. Autonomy vs compliance showed the most contradictory advice (polarity about .65), and cooperation, own vs others' interests and equality averaged near neutral because opposing advice offset each other. Results were broadly similar across the seven collections.
script.limitations: The corpus is mostly English-language, American and British proverbs, so it cannot show cross-cultural patterns. Dictionaries favor old, durable sayings over new ones. Each proverb counts once, regardless of how often people actually use it. There is no firm definition of a proverb. Ratings come mainly from an AI, and on contested dimensions like hierarchy and own-interest the AI and humans diverged, so exact positions there are uncertain. The study does not show that proverbs cause behavior.

paper.title: The cost of being seen as AI in group bargaining
paper.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.

script.description_en: Groups of three split 12 points, and opponents were tagged 'Human' or 'AI' even though everyone was human. In mixed groups, AI-tagged players earned about 18% less per round, and a gap remained even when all three agreed. It's a simplified online game, so it doesn't directly show how real AI would fare.
script.method_summary: The study ran a preregistered online bargaining game on Prolific with 2,234 analysed US participants in 776 groups of three. Each group stayed together for ten rounds. In each round, players chose cells on a triangular grid that split 12 points among the three players. Any two players holding the same cell for ten seconds finalised a deal, and the value of each point shrank over 120 seconds. Players saw each opponent labelled Human or AI but not their own label; all players were humans and made every decision. Group compositions were all-Human, one AI, two AI, or all-AI. Instructions framed the AI as either an autonomous agent or a delegate acting for a human. One random round determined a bonus. In mixed groups, AI-labelled players earned about 18% less per round (about 0.725 vs 0.879 pounds), received smaller first-offer allocations, joined fewer final deals (83.5% vs 88.2%), and earned less when included. A descriptive decomposition attributed about 71% of the gap to terms and 29% to inclusion. The gap persisted in three-player agreements and under both framings.
script.limitations: All 'AI' players were humans, so the study shows responses to labels, not how real AI agents bargain. It used a stylised game, ten rounds and one US online sample. Results are conditional on retained participants and on deals that formed. The decomposition is descriptive. Evidence on partner preference was partial, the retained-points hypothesis was not supported, and the framing comparison could not rule out a small effect. The three-player analysis was exploratory.
